source: Lawsen (2025) Comment on The Illusion of Thinking (arXiv 2506.09250 v2)
finding: Argues the Hanoi 'collapse' is an output-length and grading artefact. Models say they are shortening the output. Shojaee's River Crossing set includes unsolvable instances (N>5, boat 3). When asked for a Lua function that prints the 15-disk solution, models do it in under 5,000 tokens. The test is called 'preliminary'.
numbers: Output needs about 10 tokens per move and 2^N-1 moves, so the max solvable N is about 12-13 at a 64k limit and about 13 at 100k. Reported collapse starts before N=9, below that limit. Hanoi N=15 as code: 'very high accuracy' for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3, Gemini 2.5. No trial counts, no per-model percentages.
quote: choose not to enumerate exhaustive move lists
limits: The Lua test has no count of runs and no scores. The first version of the comment had an arithmetic error that v2 corrected. It shows the program route is plausible, not measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays only half closed. The design lesson holds: let the model write the generator and let the harness run it. But no measured pass rate at 8 to 15 disks exists in what I could open.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking, rebuttal section (arXiv 2506.06941, appendix)
finding: The authors answer the critics. They say collapse starts at N=7 and 8 (100 to 255 moves), well inside the context limit, and that the first wrong move comes early. A temperature-zero run changes nothing.
numbers: N=10 needs 1,023 moves; first failure usually within the first 100 moves (about 10%). N=8 needs 255 moves; first failure around move 40 (about 15%). They removed N>12 from Hanoi. DeepSeek-R1 at temperature 0 on Blocks World collapses at N=4; with sampling the collapse is delayed to N=30.
quote: failure occurs around 40 moves (15% of solution length)
limits: The model writes a full move list in these runs. It does not write a program. So the rebuttal answers the length objection but not the 'emit code' objection. The paper's earlier test that giving the algorithm did not help was at N=7-8.
agent_relevance: The early first-error point means slips in long in-head execution are real. That supports handing execution to a program, but it does not show that code-emitting models pass at N=8-15.

source: Tran and Kiela (2026) Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets (arXiv 2604.02460)
finding: With thinking tokens held equal, one reasoning chain (SAS) matches or beats five multi-agent layouts (sequential planner, subtask-parallel, parallel roles, debate, ensemble) on FRAMES and MuSiQue 4-hop, for Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro. Exception: at the smallest budget (100 tokens) the multi-agent variants win.
numbers: Mean accuracy over 4 models x 2 datasets. At 100 thinking tokens: SAS 0.290, Sequential 0.364, Debate 0.370, Roles 0.363. At 1000: SAS 0.418, Seq 0.379, Debate 0.388. At 2000: SAS 0.421, Seq 0.389, Debate 0.403. At 5000: SAS 0.427, Seq 0.386, Debate 0.420. At 10000: SAS 0.426, Seq 0.387, Debate 0.420. Ensemble was worst at low budgets (0.280 at 100). Bootstrap 95% CIs are in the appendix.
limits: Multi-hop QA only (no tools, no code). Under-review preprint. Gemini thinking budgets are not exactly controllable; the authors say this inflated apparent multi-agent gains. Only thinking tokens are matched, not prompt or total tokens. Self-consistency was not a separate arm (Ensemble is the nearest).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 mostly closed for pure reasoning: at equal compute, splitting into voices buys nothing and costs a little. Voices only pay when the budget is tiny or the single context is corrupted (see d04). Do not add voices to the schema for compute reasons.

source: Tran and Kiela (2026) context-degradation and error-bucket analysis (arXiv 2604.02460, section 5 and appendix)
finding: When the single chain's context is corrupted, splitting helps. On MuSiQue 4-hop with Qwen3-30B-A3B at 1000 thinking tokens, SAS leads at mild corruption (0.3), the two tie at moderate, and Sequential wins at heavy corruption (0.7). Sequential wins by exploring about twice as many entities; SAS wins by anchoring on the question text.
numbers: Gold answer string appears in thoughts: Sequential-right/SAS-wrong 41.7% vs 12.5% (Gemini Flash) and 56.7% vs 18.3% (Qwen3). SAS-right/Sequential-wrong: SAS 42.7% vs MAS 18.6% (Gemini), 63.5% vs 28.1% (Qwen3).
limits: Synthetic corruption (token deletion, replacement, random distractors). One model for the degradation sweep. No human-written noisy context.
agent_relevance: A gate for the schema: use a fresh or separate context only when the working context is long or noisy; otherwise keep one chain. Matches the idea that a program should hold clean state and give the model a fresh view.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (arXiv 2512.08296 v3)
finding: 260 configurations, 6 agent benchmarks, 5 architectures (single plus independent, centralized, decentralized, hybrid), 3 model families, tools, prompts and token budgets standardised. Multi-agent coordination helps on decomposable tasks and hurts on sequential ones. Once the single agent already scores above about 45%, extra agents give negative returns. Unchecked parallel agents amplify errors 17.2 times; a central verifier cuts that to 4.4 times.
numbers: Relative change vs single agent from +80.8% (structured finance, centralized) to -70.0% (sequential planning, independent). Planning: all multi-agent variants -39% to -70%. Capability-ceiling term beta=-0.236, p=0.004; tool-coordination term beta=-0.096, p=0.002. The 45% threshold matches 94% of cells in the authors' check. Web navigation, decentralized: +9.2%. Cross-validated R2=0.373. Best architecture predicted for 87% of held-out configurations.
limits: Google authors; compute is 'standardised' but multi-agent still fragments the per-agent budget, which the authors name as the mechanism. R2 is modest. Absolute accuracy is not predicted well, only ranking.
agent_relevance: Best available simple gate for gaps 4 and 10: if a single pass already scores above about 45% on this kind of task, or the task is a sequential chain, do not add voices or splits. Use a verifier step, not more writers.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key? (arXiv 2402.18272)
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (one worked demonstration) reaches almost the same accuracy as the best multi-agent discussion framework. Discussion beats a single agent only when the prompt has no demonstration.
numbers: Read from the abstract and the Figure 1 text (FOLIO-wiki); exact table values not extracted. The single-agent 'Demo' setting reaches an upper bound similar to all discussion frameworks.
quote: multi-agent discussion performs better than a single agent only when there is no demonstration in the prompt
limits: 2024 models; per-dataset tables not extracted. Equal-token control was not the main variable.
agent_relevance: Supports d03 and d05. Many multi-voice gains in the literature are prompt-quality gains in disguise.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate (arXiv 2502.08788 v3)
finding: Five debate methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-8B and 70B, Claude-3.5-haiku), three repeats with SDs. Debate rarely beats chain-of-thought and almost never beats self-consistency, even with far more compute. Mixing different models is the only consistent fix.
numbers: 36 model-by-dataset configurations tested by ANOVA at 0.05. SoM, EoT, ChatEval and AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of cases; MP showed no significant gain. On GPT-4o-mini, SoM lost to CoT on all 9 datasets; ChatEval and AgentVerse beat CoT on 1 of 9. On Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU only AgentVerse beat CoT (+0.85); the rest lost by at least 3.60 points. Debate beat a no-reasoning single answer in 34 of 45 GPT-4o-mini conditions. Debate did worse on programming, better on maths.
limits: Self-consistency was skipped for programming tasks. 2025 models; reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Answers the self-consistency half of gap 4: voting over independent samples is the stronger, cheaper baseline. Any multi-voice step in our schema must beat vote-of-N at equal tokens to stay.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents (arXiv 2407.01489)
finding: A fixed three-step pipeline with no tool choice by the model (localise, repair, validate) solves more of SWE-bench Lite than tool-using agents, at lower cost. So much of SWE-agent's gain can be had when the program owns the control flow.
numbers: Agentless 96 of 300 (32.00%), about $0.70 per issue. In the same table SWE-agent: 69 (23.00%) with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 55 (18.33%) with GPT-4o at $1.62; AutoCodeRover 65 (21.67%) at $2.51. The authors also drop flawed Lite problems to make Lite-S (249 problems) and find the ranking mostly holds.
limits: Table text extracted from a PDF with garbled columns; row alignment checked against the abstract (32.00%, $0.70). Different models per row. Single runs. It does not say which SWE-agent feature (lint, viewer, search) matters.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 only partly closed. Another group shows a program-owned pipeline beating model-chosen tool use on the same benchmark. It supports 'the program is the environment' but gives no feature-by-feature ablation with variance.

source: SWE-agent project (2025) mini-swe-agent README
finding: The SWE-agent authors released an agent of about 100 lines that has only a bash tool and no custom editor, viewer or linter, and recommend it as the default. They report it above 74% on SWE-bench Verified.
numbers: About 100 lines of Python; bash only; more than 74% on SWE-bench Verified (model not named on the page). No SWE-agent comparison figures on the page.
limits: Vendor README; model unnamed; Verified is a different split from the Lite (N=300) used in the 2024 ablations. Not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Boundary for gap 2: with strong 2025 models the special interface features seem less needed, which fits the capability ceiling in d05. Interface gains measured on GPT-4 Turbo may not carry to current models. Treat K04 as era-specific.

source: Anthropic (2025) The think tool: enabling Claude to stop and think (engineering blog)
finding: A tool that does nothing except give the model a place to write a note mid-task helps on policy-heavy sequential tasks and not on simple ones. The page says it adds output tokens and, from December 2025, recommends extended thinking over the tool in most cases.
numbers: tau-bench airline pass^1: table shows think+prompt 0.584, think alone 0.404, extended thinking 0.412, baseline 0.332 (text says 0.570 vs 0.370, a 54% relative gain; the page's table and text disagree). Retail pass^1: think 0.812, extended thinking 0.770, baseline 0.783. SWE-bench: think tool +1.6% on average (n=30 vs n=144, d=1.47, p<.001).
limits: Vendor blog, one model family, table and text mismatch, no equal-token control (the think arm writes more). The prompt with domain examples carried most of the airline gain (0.404 alone vs 0.584 with prompt).
agent_relevance: A fixed scratch template as a tool: small win on simple retail (+0.029), large win only with a good example prompt. Nearest thing to the gap-1 test, but not an editable-workspace vs fixed-template comparison.

source: Anthropic (2025) Managing context on the Claude Developer Platform (blog)
finding: A memory tool the agent writes to, plus a context-editing step that drops stale tool results, raised an internal agentic-search score and cut tokens in a long web-search run.
numbers: Memory tool + context editing: +39% over baseline. Context editing alone: +29%. 100-turn web search: 84% fewer tokens. Model not named for the tests; the page names Claude Sonnet 4.5 for the feature.
limits: Internal eval, no methodology, no baseline defined for the 84% figure, no variance. Vendor claim. Public beta.
agent_relevance: A weak but direct data point for gap 6: externally held notes plus pruning of old prose beat leaving everything in context. Not strong enough to cite for a number.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv 2505.06120)
finding: Across 200,000+ simulated conversations and six generation tasks, models do much worse when the instruction arrives in pieces over turns than in one message. They guess early, answer too soon, and then lean on their own earlier wrong answers. Putting all the information in one fresh message (Concat) removes the loss.
numbers: Average drop of 39% from full-instruction to sharded multi-turn. Restating earlier user turns each turn (Snowball) recovers only 15-20% of the drop; one final recap turn (Recap) recovers more but stays below the single-message Full/Concat score; tested on GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini over Code, Database, Math and Actions.
limits: Simulated user, not agents with tools. The model rereads user shards and its own answer attempts, not a program-held log. Concat is a fresh single message, the analogue of a program re-rendering state.
agent_relevance: Nearest measured analogue of gap 6: a model re-reading its own earlier prose is the failure; a clean consolidated message is the fix. Supports a program that rebuilds a fresh state view each step instead of appending to a transcript. Still no direct log-vs-prose test at equal tokens.

source: Annese et al. (2025) Who Sees What? Structured Thought-Action Sequences for Epistemic Reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2508.14564)
finding: o3-mini agents in a household Matcher-Director task. Planner-derived worked examples (goal-path, information-path, local-choice) did not reliably improve the choice to ask or look before acting. The agent ignores the cost of questions and falls back on 'grab the closest match, ask if unsure'.
numbers: 5 trials per scenario, 7 scenario types. First-take correct target: 100% in Base, Perspective-taking and Near; 0 to 40% under distractor, hidden, not-that and far (no-example: Far 20%, Distractor 40%). Average steps about 3.0 to 3.3 across example types vs planner 2.14.
limits: Tiny: 5 trials per cell, one model, percentages are multiples of 20. No equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Confirms the model chooses probes badly. It is not a measured fix. Few-shot traces did not teach the cost trade-off; an explicit belief state and cost model would be needed (the authors' own suggestion, untested).

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs (arXiv 2402.03271, abstract page)
finding: Scoring candidate questions by how much they should cut uncertainty (simulate answers, reward information gain, pick the best) improves success at 20 questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting versus direct prompting.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% across several LLMs (abstract). Per-model and per-task numbers not read.
limits: Abstract page only. The baseline named is direct prompting, so the extra simulation tokens are not matched. No cost accounting seen.
agent_relevance: The one probe-selection method with a large reported gain, and it works by a program-side expected-information-gain rule, not the model's intuition. Fits the Annese result. Unverified at equal tokens, so gap 3 stays open.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) Adaptive Tool Use in LLMs with Meta-Cognition Trigger, MeCo (arXiv 2502.12961)
finding: Asking a model whether it needs a tool is a weak gate. A gate read from the model's internal representation (MeCo) is better. In MetaTool, 50% of queries need no tool.
numbers: Decision accuracy on MetaTool, Llama3-8B: always-call 50.0%; naive self-report 61.9% (82.1% after fine-tuning, 277 calls); P(Yes) 63.5% (81.7%); MeCo 65.0% (84.3% after fine-tuning), with 206 calls before and 240 after versus 296 and 277 for naive. A search call costs 14.8 s on MeCa-RAG.
limits: Needs access to hidden states; measures the decision, not end accuracy on the task. Single runs.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a prompted 'do I need a tool?' answer is only a little better than always calling. A gate should use something measured outside the model's words (calibrated confidence, cheap pre-check). The end-task accuracy cost of over-calling is not shown here.

source: Hesselmann (2020) No conclusive evidence that difficult general knowledge questions cause a Google Stroop effect (PeerJ 8:e10325, PMC7651475)
finding: Second replication of Sparrow, Liu and Wegner 2011 Experiment 1 (the Stroop-type test, not the memory test). Camerer 2018 also failed on it. This one failed too.
numbers: N=117 tested, 89 in the final analysis. Original N=46; Camerer's replication N=104 in stage 1 and 234 pooled. Easy-block RT 830 ms general vs 901 ms computer words; hard-block 825 vs 821 ms. Sequential Bayes factor BF01=5.07 for the null; with the original pattern as the alternative BF0+=16.43. Preregistered t(88)=-1.04, p=.301. Trivia accuracy 97% easy, 60% hard (original 98% vs 47%).
limits: German student-project sample. The original author (Sparrow 2018) criticised Camerer's block-wise load manipulation; this study used the per-word design and still got a null. Memory results (Experiments 2-4) were not re-tested.
agent_relevance: The Sparrow priming result is not reliable; cite it only as contested. The 'we offload and remember less' idea rests on other evidence, and for agents it is design reasoning, not human data.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science, 2010-2015 (Nat Hum Behav; nature.com page)
finding: 21 experiments replicated at about five times original power. Sparrow et al. 2011 'Google effects on memory' is one of the 21.
numbers: 13 of 21 (62%) showed a significant effect in the same direction; replication effect sizes averaged about 50% of the originals; indicator range 12 to 14 of 21 (57% to 67%); Bayesian true-positive estimate 67%. Per-study Sparrow figures are in figures and supplement I could not read.
limits: The Sparrow row was not read. The null is taken from Hesselmann's account (d16) and a Wikipedia summary (d21). The page text had no tables.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: the replication rate in this set is 62%, and Sparrow's Experiment 1 is among the failures.

source: Ruiz Pardo and Minda (2021 preprint) Reexamining the Brain Drain Effect: Does Ward et al. (2017) Replicate? (PsyArXiv 5y34g)
finding: Preregistered direct replication of Ward et al. 2017 Experiment 2: phone on desk, in pocket/bag, or outside the room, crossed with phone on or off (six cells). Operation-span and go/no-go tasks. No effect of phone location or power.
numbers: N=383 analysed (44 excluded); cell n=58 to 70. OSpan location F(2,377)=0.10, p=.91, partial eta2=.001; power F(1,377)=0.21, p=.65, eta2=.001. Go/no-go location x cue-type interaction F(2,377)=3.19, p=.04 (the only hit, uncorrected). Moderators (dependency, attachment) did not change the null (R2 .004 to .01).
limits: I read the preprint, not the journal version. I did not read Ward 2017 itself (403), so original effect sizes are not recorded. Student participants.
agent_relevance: Closes most of the 'mere presence of a phone drains cognition' story for design purposes. Do not borrow it as evidence for an agent rule.

source: Meta-analysis (2023) Does the mere presence of a smartphone impact cognitive performance? A meta-analysis of the brain drain effect (Media Psychology; OSF tnyda abstract)
finding: Six meta-analyses on 56 effects and 7,093 participants. Only working-memory capacity showed a significant pooled harm; the other functions were null. Power was poor and methods varied.
numbers: k=56, n=7,093; one of six pooled effects significant (working memory). Pooled g not read from the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. The earlier meta-analysis in the claims (22 studies, 43 effects) is a different set.
agent_relevance: With d18, the human offloading-harm family is small and fragile at best. Keep K11 at weak.

source: Martin and Schwartz (2005) Physically Distributed Learning (Cognitive Science 29:587-625; Crossref abstract)
finding: Five studies with 9- and 10-year-olds on fractions. Moving physical pieces helped them build a meaning for fractions. Experiments 4 and 5: children who adapted a loosely structured set of materials transferred to new materials better than children who used well-structured materials that did not need adapting.
numbers: No numbers: only the abstract was read (the full paper was behind a paywall; Stanford URLs returned 404 and the publisher 403). Five experiments; ages 9-10.
quote: the opportunity to adapt an environment permits the development of new interpretations that can advance learning
limits: Abstract only. Effect sizes, group sizes and the transfer gap are not recorded. Human children, a physical task.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the human basis for letting the agent edit its own workspace. The claim is about transfer, not speed. The agent test would be an editable scratch file vs a fixed template at equal tokens, scored on a changed problem. No such LLM study found in this pass.

source: Wikipedia (2025) Google effect, replication section
finding: Secondary summary of what followed Sparrow 2011: Camerer 2018 could not replicate, Hesselmann 2020 found no conclusive evidence, Schooler and Storm 2021 found the effect only when people had experience that saved information stays accessible, and Gong and Yang 2024 meta-analysed 35 studies.
numbers: Camerer: 21 studies. Gong and Yang 2024: 35 studies, supporting a link between frequent searching and memory changes. No effect sizes on the page.
limits: Encyclopedia page; the first 100,000 characters were read. Use only as a pointer. Schooler and Storm and Gong and Yang were not opened.
agent_relevance: Adds one boundary condition for offloading effects on memory: the person must trust that the store will persist. For an agent that is built in if the program-held log is reliable.

source: Hutchins (1995) Cognition in the Wild, full text on Internet Archive (cognitioninwild0000hutc)
finding: Attempt to read the book text to check the calculator claim and any navigation error rate failed: the lending-library text returned HTTP 401. I did not work around it.
numbers: none
limits: Not opened. The calculator-in-the-emergency-fix claim and any measured error rate for the navigation team remain unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. K18 should stay qualitative and unverified.
